title: The Future of At-home Diagnostics
summary: denise-ellison
body_text: At-home diagnostic testing refers to the practice of individuals administering medical tests in their own homes without the assistance of a healthcare professional. In recent years, advances in technology have made it easier for individuals to perform medical tests at home, leading to a growing demand for this type of testing. At-home testing can provide numerous benefits, including improved convenience, cost-effectiveness, and privacy. However, one of the most significant benefits of at-home testing is the relief it can provide to overworked medical professionals. Medical professionals are under increasing pressure due to the increasing demand for their services. This demand is driven by factors such as an aging population, a growing prevalence of chronic conditions, and an increasing number of patients seeking medical care. As a result, medical professionals are becoming increasingly overworked, which can lead to burnout, decreased job satisfaction, and a decrease in the quality of care provided to patients. At-home diagnostic testing can help relieve overworked medical professionals in several ways. Firstly, it can reduce the number of patients who need to visit a doctor's office or hospital for testing. By allowing individuals to perform tests in the privacy and comfort of their own homes, at-home testing reduces the burden on medical professionals who would otherwise need to perform these tests. Additionally, at-home testing eliminates the need for individuals to take time off work or wait in line at a doctor's office, making the testing process more efficient and convenient. Secondly, at-home diagnostic testing can improve the accuracy of test results. By eliminating the need for medical professionals to perform tests, the risk of human error is reduced, leading to more accurate results. Additionally, at-home testing can improve the speed of test results, as individuals can perform tests at their convenience and send the results to their healthcare provider for analysis. This can lead to faster diagnoses and treatments, improving the overall quality of care provided to patients. Finally, at-home diagnostic testing can improve patient outcomes by providing individuals with greater control over their own health. By allowing individuals to monitor their own health, at-home testing can improve patient engagement and encourage individuals to take a more active role in their own healthcare. This can lead to better health outcomes, as individuals are more likely to identify and address health problems early on. At-home diagnostic testing can also provide medical professionals with valuable insights into their patients’ health, allowing them to make more informed decisions about diagnoses and treatments. By providing medical professionals with a more complete picture of their patients’ health, at-home testing can improve the quality of care provided to patients and relieve the burden on medical professionals. It is important to note that at-home diagnostic testing is not a replacement for traditional medical care, but rather a complement to it. Medical professionals still play a critical role in the diagnosis and treatment of medical conditions, and at-home testing should never be used as a substitute for professional medical care. However, by relieving some of the burden on medical professionals, at-home testing can help improve the quality of care provided to patients. In order to ensure the safe and effective use of at-home diagnostic testing, it is important that individuals receive proper training on how to perform the tests correctly. This can be achieved through a combination of written instructions, videos, and training sessions with healthcare professionals. Additionally, it is important that individuals receive access to reliable and accurate test results, which can be achieved through the use of high-quality testing equipment and the use of telemedicine services. In conclusion, at-home diagnostic testing can play an important role in relieving overworked medical professionals by reducing the number of patients who need to visit a doctor's office or hospital for testing, improving the accuracy and speed of test results, and encouraging individuals to take a more active role in their own healthcare. While at-home testing is not a replacement for traditional medical care, it can complement it and help improve the overall quality of care provided to patients. However, it is important to ensure the safe and effective use of at-home diagnostic testing by providing individuals with proper training and access to reliable and accurate test results. As the demand for medical services continues to grow, it is likely that the use of at-home diagnostic testing will continue to increase in the coming years. This trend is likely to bring numerous benefits to patients, medical professionals, and the healthcare system as a whole. By reducing the burden on medical professionals, at-home testing can help ensure that patients receive the high-quality care they need and deserve. In the next decade, it is likely that we will see continued growth and development in the field of at-home diagnostic testing. As technology continues to advance, it is likely that we will see more and more tests become available for at-home use, providing individuals with greater access to medical testing and improving the overall quality of care provided to patients. Additionally, it is likely that we will see the development of new and innovative telemedicine services, which will further improve the accuracy, speed, and convenience of at-home diagnostic testing. Overall, at-home diagnostic testing has the potential to revolutionize the way medical testing is performed, and to relieve the burden on overworked medical professionals. By providing individuals with greater control over their own health and improving the quality of care provided to patients, at-home testing has the potential to improve the lives of millions of people around the world. In summary, at-home diagnostic testing can relieve overworked medical professionals by reducing the number of patients who need to visit a doctor's office or hospital for testing, improving the accuracy and speed of test results, and encouraging individuals to take a more active role in their own healthcare. As technology continues to advance, it is likely that we will see continued growth and development in the field of at-home diagnostic testing, providing individuals with greater access to medical testing and improving the overall quality of care provided to patients. ‍

title: In-House vs. Managed Vendor Portals: Which Approach Is Right for Your Business?
summary: In-house vs. managed vendor portals: compare cost, control, and scalability to choose the right fit for your business.
body_text: In this article, learn about: What a vendor portal is and why retailers use one The differences between in-house and managed vendor portals The advantages and limitations of each approach Factors to consider when choosing the right solution for your business Vendor portals have become an essential part of modern retail operations. They simplify supplier communication, support the exchange of purchase orders (POs), invoices, advance ship notices (ASNs), and product data, and provide a central source of truth for supplier information at a time when 47% of procurement leaders say they don't fully trust the supplier data they rely on. Once a retailer decides it needs a vendor portal, the next decision is whether to build and manage the platform internally or work with a managed provider. Both approaches can be successful, but they come with different tradeoffs. Internal IT resources, supplier onboarding, long-term maintenance, scalability, and evolving compliance requirements all influence which model makes the most sense. Understanding those tradeoffs can help retailers choose a solution that supports both today's operations and future growth. What Is a Vendor Portal? A vendor portal is the system that retailers and their suppliers use to exchange day-to-day documents that keep goods moving: POs, ASNs, invoices, and product data. Instead of emailing spreadsheets, suppliers log in (or connect via EDI or API ) to send and receive these documents in a structured, trackable way. Why Retailers Implement Vendor Portals As retailers demand faster onboarding, stricter compliance, richer product data and greater visibility across their supply chains, the portal has come to serve as the operational hub connecting suppliers to retailer requirements. Choosing the right model today can influence how quickly a business adapts tomorrow. These portals replace manual, error-prone communication with a consistent process across every supplier relationship. The most common use cases include: Electronic POs) : Sending and confirming orders without phone calls or manual re-entry ASNs) : Giving warehouses advance visibility into what's arriving and when Invoices: Matching supplier invoices to POs and receipts to reduce disputes and speed up payment Product information : Keeping item attributes, pricing, and packaging data current across the network Supplier onboarding: Bringing new vendors up to speed on requirements, formats, and expectations Handled well, these five functions cut down on chargebacks , late shipments, and the kind of manual follow-up that consumes a buying team's week. Handled poorly, they become the reason for missed deadlines and sales. Option 1: In-House Vendor Portals An in-house vendor portal is one your organization builds, hosts, and maintains internally, typically with your own development and IT teams. Advantages Building an in-house vendor portal gives you full control. You decide the feature set, the user experience, and the pace of change. If your business has unusual requirements, like a proprietary ERP integration or a workflow no off-the-shelf tool supports, an in-house build can be shaped exactly to fit. Disadvantages That control comes at a cost. Every update, security patch, and new supplier requirement becomes a development project. As your supplier base grows, so does the maintenance burden, and the team that built the portal may not be the team available to keep improving it years later. Best Fit In-house portals tend to make the most sense for larger retailers with dedicated software development teams, highly specific workflow requirements, and the internal capacity to treat the portal as a permanent product, not a side project. What Ongoing Ownership Looks Like IT ownership: Your team owns uptime, security, issue resolution, and every feature request that comes in from buyers or suppliers. Ongoing maintenance: Updates to compliance rules, retailer requirements, or supplier onboarding flows require internal development time. Scalability: Supporting more suppliers, more transaction volume, or new connectivity requirements is your team's responsibility to plan and build for. Related Reading: How to Generate a Best-In-Class Compliance Program Option 2: Managed Vendor Portals A managed vendor portal is built, hosted, and continuously updated by an outside provider. External teams configure it to the business rules; the provider handles the infrastructure, updates, and supplier-facing support. Advantages Managed portals shift the operational weight off your team. Updates roll out automatically, supplier support has somewhere to go besides your help desk, and new suppliers can typically be onboarded in days rather than months, since the connectivity and testing process is already established. Disadvantages Managed portals trade some customization for speed and reliability. You're working within the provider's network and product direction, which means less flexibility for highly specific internal workflows. You're also relying on that provider's uptime, support quality, and pace of innovation, so the choice of provider matters as much as the choice of model. Best Fit Managed portals tend to work best for retailers who want to move quickly, don't have the internal development capacity to treat a portal as a long-term software product, and support a supplier base that spans a wide range of technical sophistication. What the Experience Looks Like Managed updates: Compliance changes and new requirements are handled by the provider and rolled out across the network. Supplier support: Suppliers get dedicated onboarding and troubleshooting help instead of relying on your internal team. Faster onboarding: New suppliers connect through an established process rather than a custom-built one. Side-by-Side Comparison Feature In-House Managed Initial investment Higher Lower Ongoing maintenance Internal Provider-managed Scalability Internal responsibility Managed by provider Supplier onboarding Internal team Managed service Updates Internal Continuous IT resources Significant Minimal Consider the Total Cost of Ownership Initial implementation costs are only part of the equation. The total cost of ownership (TCO) includes ongoing maintenance, software updates, security patches, infrastructure, supplier support, compliance changes, and the internal time required to keep the portal running effectively. While an in-house portal can offer greater control and customization, those benefits come with long-term operational responsibilities. A managed vendor portal shifts much of that work to the provider, allowing internal teams to focus on strategic initiatives rather than maintaining the platform itself. When evaluating your options, consider not only what the portal costs to build or subscribe to today, but also what it will cost to operate over the next several years. Related Reading: Maintaining Data Accuracy as Order Volume Grows How to Choose Rather than treating one option as universally better, work through a few honest questions about your business: Do you have dedicated IT resources who can treat the portal as an ongoing product (not a one-time project)? How quickly do you need to onboard suppliers , and can your current process support that speed? How often do your requirements change , whether that's compliance rules, retailer routing guides, or data formats? Are you supporting dozens of suppliers or hundreds? Scale changes what "manageable” means. There's no wrong answer here. Some retailers genuinely need the control of an in-house build. Many more find that the speed, consistency, and reduced internal burden of a managed portal fits where their business is today. Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Vendor Portals What is the difference between an in-house vendor portal and a managed vendor portal? An in-house vendor portal is built, hosted and maintained by the retailer, giving the organization full control over the platform but also responsibility for ongoing maintenance, updates and support. A managed vendor portal is operated by a third-party provider, which handles hosting, supplier onboarding, maintenance and system updates while allowing retailers to focus on their core business. What are the benefits of using a managed vendor portal? Managed vendor portals can help retailers accelerate supplier onboarding, reduce IT maintenance, improve supplier adoption, and adapt more quickly to changing business requirements. Because the provider manages the platform and ongoing support, retailers can scale more efficiently without investing in additional infrastructure or internal resources. How do vendor portals improve supplier collaboration? Vendor portals provide a centralized location where suppliers can receive purchase orders, submit invoices, share product information, and exchange shipping documents such as ASNs. By giving both retailers and suppliers access to accurate, up-to-date information, vendor portals reduce manual work, improve visibility, and support more efficient collaboration across the supply chain. How SPS Commerce Helps SPS Commerce operates as a managed vendor portal, built around a network of 300,000+ trading relationships and 400+ system partners rather than a single custom deployment. When a compliance rule changes, it's detected, updated, and applied once, for everyone on the network , instead of triggering a separate development cycle for each retailer. Onboarding is handled the same way. Rather than leaving suppliers to figure out connectivity on their own, structured onboarding and readiness support brings new suppliers up to speed with testing, certification, and go-live coordination managed by dedicated advisors. Retailers get a portal that scales with supplier count without scaling their internal IT workload alongside it. The right model still depends on your business. But for most retailers weighing the ongoing cost of building versus the value of a system that's already proven across a large trading network, a managed vendor portal is worth a serious look. Questions like this come up often as retail operations evolve. Explore The Source , free to sign up, for more supply chain education like this to help guide decisions as your business grows.

title: Can an AI Interviewer Reduce Bias in Technical Hiring?
summary: Bias in technical hiring is well documented: identical resumes get evaluated differently based on the...
body_text: Hiring Best Practices Can an AI Interviewer Reduce Bias in Technical Hiring? Written By Danielle Bechtel | July 17, 2026 Bias in technical hiring is well documented: identical resumes get evaluated differently based on the name at the top, interview panels are more likely to advance candidates who remind them of themselves, and interview rigor can vary widely depending on who’s asking the questions and how their day is going. An AI interviewer, used well, can address some of these problems, but it isn’t a silver bullet, and it can introduce its own risks if implemented carelessly. This article looks at where AI interviewers genuinely help reduce bias, where the evidence is more mixed, and what hiring teams should do to make sure automation improves fairness rather than just moving it somewhere less visible. Where Human Interview Bias Shows Up Before evaluating whether AI helps, it’s worth naming the specific failure modes it’s meant to address: Inconsistent rigor. The same candidate might face a tougher or easier bar depending on which interviewer they’re assigned, how many interviews that person has already done that day, or unconscious affinity bias toward candidates with a similar background. Halo and horn effects. An early strong or weak impression, sometimes based on something as irrelevant as small talk at the start of a call, can color how an interviewer scores the rest of the conversation. Non-standardized questions. When interviewers are free to ask whatever they want, candidates aren’t actually being evaluated against the same bar, which makes comparisons across candidates unreliable and easier to skew by bias. Confirmation bias in scoring. Interviewers sometimes score in a way that confirms an impression they’d already formed from the resume or a screening call, rather than the actual interview performance. How AI Interviewers Can Help Standardized question sets. A well-configured AI interviewer asks every candidate a comparable set of questions for a given role, removing the variability that comes from one interviewer improvising while another follows a script closely. Rubric-based scoring. Instead of a holistic “gut feeling” score, AI interviewers typically evaluate responses against defined criteria, correctness, approach, communication, applied the same way across every candidate. No fatigue effects. A human interviewer’s fifth interview of the day is not evaluated with the same freshness as their first. An AI interviewer doesn’t get tired, distracted, or impatient. Auditable scoring patterns. Because AI interviewer output is structured and logged, hiring teams can actually run statistical checks on outcomes, for example, whether pass rates differ meaningfully across demographic groups, in a way that’s far harder to do with dozens of individual human interviewers whose reasoning isn’t recorded in detail. Where the Evidence Is More Mixed AI models can inherit bias from training data. If a model was trained or fine-tuned on historical hiring data that reflects past discriminatory patterns, it can reproduce those patterns unless specifically corrected for. Bias mitigation has to be a deliberate design choice, not an assumption. Communication style bias. Some AI evaluation systems have been shown to favor certain speech patterns, accents, or communication styles, which risks disadvantaging candidates who are highly skilled but communicate differently than the model’s training data would predict as “typical.” This is an active area of scrutiny across the industry. Reduced human context. A human interviewer might recognize that a nontraditional background, a bootcamp grad, a career-changer, a candidate from a non-target school, doesn’t reflect ability. A poorly designed AI interviewer, scoring rigidly against a rubric calibrated on traditional backgrounds, could penalize exactly the kind of candidate a more thoughtful process would want to advance. What “Doing This Well” Actually Looks Like Reducing bias with an AI interviewer isn’t automatic. It requires specific practices: Regular bias audits. Track pass-through rates by demographic group at each stage where the AI interviewer is involved, and investigate meaningful disparities rather than assuming the system is neutral by default. Rubrics built around skills, not pattern-matching to “ideal” answers. Scoring should reward correct reasoning and problem-solving, not superficial similarity to a reference answer. Human review of edge cases. Borderline scores, or candidates flagged as low-confidence by the model, should route to human review rather than being auto-rejected. Transparency with candidates. Candidates should know when they’re interacting with an AI interviewer and have a clear path to raise concerns or request a human review of their evaluation. Diverse validation data. Before deploying an AI interviewer broadly, test it against a diverse set of past candidates and outcomes to check whether scoring holds up consistently across groups. A Balanced Take The honest answer to “does an AI interviewer reduce bias?” is: it can, but only if it’s built and monitored deliberately. The consistency and standardization that AI brings genuinely address some of the most common sources of human interview bias — inconsistent rigor, fatigue, and improvised questioning. But AI systems are not automatically fair just because they’re not human, and organizations that treat automation as a bias-reduction feature without ongoing auditing risk trading one set of problems for another, less visible one. Practical Takeaway If reducing bias is a driving reason for adopting an AI interviewer, treat it as an ongoing program, not a one-time implementation decision. That means auditing outcomes regularly, keeping a human review path for edge cases, and being transparent with candidates about how they’re being evaluated. Done this way, AI interviewers can be a meaningful step toward more consistent, defensible technical hiring, not just a faster version of the same process. HackerRank built Chakra to fight bias. title: 25 HR Leaders in MENA Reshaping How Talent Works in the AI Era
summary: 25 HR leaders in MENA rewriting talent strategy for the AI era and shaping the Gulf's future of work.
body_text: The most influential HR leaders in MENA are no longer the ones who run payroll cleanly. Ten years ago, HR in this region ran payroll, processed leave, and closed the file. It was a service desk with a headcount. That job is gone. The same function now decides whether AI screens candidates, how performance gets measured when half the work happens next to a model, and what “a career” means to a 24-year-old in Riyadh who has never known a workplace without automation. The stakes moved from administrative to existential, and a specific group of people moved with it. The 25 leaders below made that jump early. Most are not on the conference circuit. They are running the actual work inside places like Aramco Digital, GE Vernova, Huda Beauty, and the giga-projects redrawing Saudi Arabia. Some are widely followed already. Several deserve more attention than they get. Here is who they are, and what their choices signal about where the profession is going. Why MENA is where the AI-and-talent question gets answered first Most regions are still debating whether AI belongs in the workplace. MENA skipped that debate. Vision 2030 put a national deadline on workforce transformation. The Gulf’s giga-projects need to hire, train, and deploy tens of thousands of people faster than any traditional HR model allows. The workforce here also skews young and digital-first in a way that makes “pilot it next year” an unaffordable answer. When a country decides to build a new city, the people’s strategy cannot lag the construction schedule. That kind of pressure produces a particular kind of HR leader: one who treats AI as an operating reality, not a panel topic. The people on this list did not wait for a global best practice to emerge. They wrote it. Which is why watching this specific cohort matters more than most. Where they land is where the profession lands six months later. How these 25 HR leaders were chosen This is not a popularity contest and it is not pay-to-play. Three things decided the list. Seniority with real scope: people leading the HR or people function at a recognized organization, with responsibility for strategy rather than administration. An active voice on the questions that matter now, especially where AI, culture, and performance intersect. And regional influence: leaders whose decisions ripple beyond their own org chart, across the Gulf and the wider Middle East. The 25 are numbered but grouped into five clusters, not ranked. title: ETF à effet de levier : définition et fonctionnement
summary: ETF à effet de levier : définition, fonctionnement, risques et exemples (CAC 40, S&P 500, Nasdaq) pour investisseurs avertis en court terme.
body_text: Mis à jour le 21 juillet 2026 Un ETF à effet de levier est un fonds coté qui multiplie chaque jour les variations, à la hausse comme à la baisse, d'un indice sous-jacent, généralement par un facteur de 2 ou 3. Réservé aux investisseurs avertis pour du très court terme, il comporte un risque élevé de perte en capital. L'essentiel Un ETF à levier 2x ou 3x amplifie les gains et les pertes quotidiennes de son indice de référence, dans un ratio fixe. Le rebalancement quotidien génère un effet d'érosion (beta slippage) qui peut réduire la performance sur plusieurs jours, même si l'indice termine stable. Certains ETF à effet de levier sur le CAC 40 ou le Nasdaq-100 sont éligibles au PEA grâce à une structure synthétique conforme, malgré leur exposition à effet de levier. Ces produits sont conçus pour une détention de quelques heures à quelques jours, pas comme un placement de long terme. Qu’est-ce qu’un ETF à effet de levier ? Un ETF à effet de levier est un fonds négocié en bourse conçu pour amplifier les rendements quotidiens d'un indice ou d'un actif sous-jacent. Contrairement aux ETF traditionnels qui reflètent directement les mouvements de leur indice, les ETF à effet de levier multiplient les gains et les pertes, souvent dans un ratio de 2:1 ou 3:1. Les ETF à effet de levier utilisent des produits dérivés tels que les options et les contrats à terme pour atteindre cet objectif. Cela permet à ces fonds de viser un multiple des performances de leur indice sous-jacent . Exemple de Fonctionnement Indice sous-jacent augmente de 1 % : ETF à effet de levier 2x : +2 % ETF à effet de levier 3x : +3 % Indice sous-jacent diminue de 1 % : ETF à effet de levier 2x : -2 % ETF à effet de levier 3x : -3 % Centralisez votre patrimoine PEA, livrets d'épargne, cryptomonnaies, actions, immobilier, comptes bancaires. Découvrir Finary Comment un ETF à effet de levier prend de la valeur ? Un ETF à effet de levier se base sur la performance journalière de son indice de référence. Lorsque l'indice monte, l'ETF à effet de levier augmente ses rendements quotidiens de manière multipliée. Par exemple, un ETF à levier 2x sur le CAC 40 amplifiera une augmentation de 1 % pour générer une hausse de 2 %. Composition et ajustements de l'ETF L'ETF emprunte des fonds ou utilise des produits dérivés pour amplifier les mouvements. Chaque jour, il réajuste ses positions pour maintenir le levier souhaité, ce qui peut éroder les gains sur le long terme en raison de la volatilité. Impact des mouvements de marché Hausse : Lorsqu'un marché est en hausse constante, l'ETF multipliant cette croissance peut générer des gains amplifiés, mais l'inverse est tout aussi vrai en cas de baisse. Baisse : À l'inverse, si le marché baisse, la perte est également amplifiée, ce qui peut rapidement diminuer la valeur de l'investissement. Volatilité et rendements quotidiens La volatilité influence grandement les rendements quotidiens. Les mouvements constants de haut en bas peuvent user les performances positives dues aux ajustements quotidiens. C'est essentiel pour les investisseurs de comprendre qu'un marché très volatile peut rendre les stratégies à effet de levier imprévisibles sur le long terme. Attention : Un autre aspect important à considérer est la nature risquée de ces produits. Investir dans des ETF à effet de levier comporte un risque accru de pertes, pouvant aller jusqu'à la perte totale du capital investi. Quels sont les avantages des ETF à effet de levier ? Les ETF à effet de levier offrent une amplification des gains potentiels à court terme, un outil flexible pour les traders actifs et un accès à des stratégies auparavant réservées aux investisseurs institutionnels, au prix d'un risque de perte accru. Une amplification potentielle des variations à court terme Les ETF à effet de levier utilisent la dette pour multiplier les mouvements des indices sous-jacents, ce qui amplifie autant les gains potentiels que les pertes sur de courtes périodes. Un outil polyvalent pour les traders actifs Ces fonds sont adaptés à diverses stratégies de trading actif, incluant : Day trading Hedging Spéculation sur les mouvements de marché à court terme Une nouvelle façon de diversifier son portefeuille Les ETF à effet de levier permettent d'obtenir une exposition amplifiée à des indices spécifiques (S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, CAC 40), avec un risque proportionnellement accru. Des stratégies complexes à portée de main Ces produits offrent aux investisseurs particuliers un accès à des stratégies d'investissement complexes, traditionnellement réservées aux investisseurs institutionnels. Une liquidité qui facilite les transactions rapides La plupart des ETF à effet de levier sont très liquides, permettant des entrées et sorties rapides de positions. Il est crucial de bien comprendre les risques associés avant d'investir dans ces produits sophistiqués. ‍ Quels sont les risques associés aux ETF à effet de levier ? Les ETF à effet de levier exposent l'investisseur à une volatilité amplifiée, une érosion des performances sur le long terme (beta slippage) et un risque de perte pouvant atteindre la totalité du capital investi. Une volatilité grandement amplifiée Les ETF à effet de levier augmentent la volatilité par rapport aux ETF traditionnels. Une baisse de 1% du marché peut entraîner une perte de 2% ou plus pour un ETF à double levier. Cette amplification accroît le risque de pertes importantes, surtout en période de turbulences du marché. Une érosion des performances à long terme Le réajustement quotidien de ces ETF peut réduire les rendements sur le long terme. Ce phénomène, appelé "beta slippage", peut diminuer la valeur de l'investissement même si le marché est stable. Les ajustements fréquents génèrent des coûts supplémentaires qui impactent la performance globale. Un niveau de risque élevé Ces produits présentent un risque nettement supérieur aux ETF classiques. Ils sont conçus pour des investisseurs expérimentés qui comprennent parfaitement les mécanismes sous-jacents. Une gestion inadéquate peut rapidement amplifier les pertes initiales. Une complexité nécessitant une compréhension approfondie Il est essentiel de bien comprendre le fonctionnement des ETF à effet de levier avant d'investir. Les émetteurs fournissent des prospectus détaillés que l'investisseur doit étudier attentivement. Cette compréhension doit inclure la mécanique de l'effet de levier, les frais associés et les différents scénarios de performance possibles. Ici, les traders cherchent à tirer parti des mouvements de prix au cours d'une seule journée. Compréhension du mécanisme Les ETF à effet de levier visent à multiplier les rendements quotidiens d'un indice sous-jacent. Un ETF 2x cherche à doubler la performance journalière de l'indice, tandis qu'un ETF -2x vise à offrir le double de la performance inverse. Rebalancement quotidien Ces ETF sont rebalancés quotidiennement, ce qui peut entraîner un écart de performance sur le long terme par rapport à l'indice sous-jacent. Ce phénomène, appelé "decay" ou "beta slippage", est crucial à comprendre pour les traders. Stratégies de trading Momentum trading : Profiter des tendances fortes à court terme en utilisant des ETF à effet de levier dans le sens du mouvement. Mean reversion : Parier sur le retour à la moyenne des indices après des mouvements extrêmes, en utilisant des ETF inverses. Hedging : Utiliser des ETF inverses pour protéger un portefeuille contre les baisses de marché à court terme. Gestion des risques Utiliser des stop-loss serrés est crucial en raison de la volatilité accrue. Il est recommandé de limiter l'exposition aux ETF à effet de levier à un faible pourcentage du portefeuille total. Surveillance du marché Les traders doivent suivre de près les facteurs influençant l'indice sous-jacent, tels que les annonces économiques, les résultats d'entreprises et les événements géopolitiques. Importance du timing L'entrée et la sortie des positions sont critiques en raison de l'effet de levier. Les traders doivent être prêts à agir rapidement en fonction de l'évolution du marché. Gestion des ETF à effet de levier et considérations fiscales Les ETF à effet de levier requièrent une gestion rigoureuse en raison de leur nature amplificatrice. Ces produits financiers multiplient les gains et les pertes de l'indice sous-jacent. Il est donc crucial de bien connaître les frais de gestion et autres coûts . Les frais de gestion des ETF à effet de levier peuvent varier, mais sont souvent plus élevés que ceux des ETF traditionnels. Il est important de les comparer entre différents produits et courtiers . Ils ne doivent donc pas constituer l'intégralité d'un portefeuille. L'ETF à effet de levier peut être éligible au PEA (Plan d'Épargne en Actions) , mais il faut vérifier les conditions spécifiques auprès de son courtier ou de sa société de gestion . Tous les ETF ne sont pas compatibles avec ce type de placement. Certains ETF à effet de levier sur le CAC 40 ou le Nasdaq-100 sont ainsi éligibles au PEA malgré leur exposition à un indice ou un levier non européen : leur structure synthétique conserve un panier d'actions européennes éligibles tout en répliquant la performance visée via un swap, ce qui respecte la règle des 75 % d'actions de l'Union européenne. Le SRD (Service de Règlement Différé) permet d'opérer avec un effet de levier sur certaines transactions, ce qui amplifie également les pertes potentielles. Ce dispositif est réservé aux investisseurs avertis. Considérations fiscales : Impôt sur les plus-values : Les gains réalisés sont soumis à l'impôt sur les plus-values mobilières. Dividendes perçus : Ils peuvent être soumis à l'impôt sur le revenu. Frais de transaction : Ils doivent être pris en compte dans le calcul des rendements nets. Stratégies alternatives utilisant des ETF à effet de levier Les ETF à effet de levier peuvent être combinés à d'autres instruments dans le cadre de stratégies actives, qui comportent toutes un risque de perte élevé. Une approche consiste à utiliser les contrats à terme . Ces instruments permettent d'augmenter les gains potentiels en répliquant les mouvements d'un indice avec un levier de 2 ou 3 fois. Les options sont une autre stratégie alternative. Elles donnent aux investisseurs la possibilité d'acheter ou de vendre des ETF à un prix prédéterminé, offrant ainsi plus de flexibilité dans la gestion du risque. Les CFD (Contrats pour la Différence) sont des produits dérivés à haut risque. Selon l' ESMA , l'autorité européenne des marchés financiers, entre 74 % et 89 % des comptes d'investisseurs particuliers perdent de l'argent en négociant des CFD. Les produits dérivés tels que les contrats dérivés permettent d'amplifier les rendements. Toutefois, ces instruments financiers peuvent également augmenter les risques. Une autre stratégie implique d'employer la dette . Investir à crédit dans des produits à effet de levier est une pratique extrêmement risquée qui peut conduire à des pertes supérieures au capital initial et n'est pas recommandée. Ce n'est toutefois pas systématique : il faut vérifier l'éligibilité auprès de son courtier ou sur la fiche DICI de chaque fonds avant d'investir. Peut-on garder un ETF à effet de levier sur le long terme ? Non, ces produits sont conçus pour une exposition de très court terme. Le rebalancement quotidien entraîne un phénomène d'érosion appelé beta slippage, qui peut faire perdre de la valeur à l'ETF même si l'indice sous-jacent termine stable ou en légère hausse sur plusieurs jours. Quelle est la différence entre un ETF à effet de levier et un ETF classique ? Un ETF classique réplique fidèlement la performance de son indice, tandis qu'un ETF à effet de levier multiplie sa variation quotidienne par un facteur fixe, généralement 2 ou 3. Cette amplification s'applique aussi bien aux gains qu'aux pertes, ce qui augmente fortement le risque. Quel est le risque maximal d'un ETF à effet de levier ? Le risque de perte peut atteindre la totalité du capital investi. La combinaison de l'amplification quotidienne et de la volatilité des marchés peut entraîner des pertes rapides et importantes, en particulier en cas de détention prolongée ou de forte instabilité du marché. Les ETF à effet de levier sont-ils adaptés aux débutants ? Non, ces produits s'adressent à des investisseurs avertis, capables de suivre leurs positions quotidiennement et de comprendre des mécanismes comme le rebalancement ou le beta slippage. Pour un débutant, un ETF classique et diversifié reste une option plus adaptée pour investir en bourse. title: A Taxonomy of Agent Failures
summary: Seven silent failure modes that execution monitoring misses, and the boundary that separates them from every signal in the span.
body_text: An action cannot tell you whether it was correct. It cannot tell you whether it fulfilled the request, violated an instruction, repeated a failed attempt, relied on something false, or left the user convinced nothing happened. Correctness depends on information the action itself doesn't contain. Yet most production monitoring still evaluates agent actions as though the span contains everything needed to judge correctness. Imagine you have an agent in production. Users are churning. You pull up the traces: thousands of them. Latency, error rates, cost analyses. All look fine. Something is wrong and there's nowhere to look. That's the actual problem. Traditional software usually failed in ways you could observe, such as an exception, timeout, or a crash. AI agents don't. Often, they return successfully while the failure stays concealed. That's what we mean by silent failure . The agent appears to succeed, but the intended work never happened, or happened incorrectly. It may ignore part of the user's request, continue after a critical tool fails, or invent a record and log it as complete. An agent that skips half its work and reports back 'done' has no name for what went wrong, so it gets logged as a success and shows up three weeks later as churn. We've spent the last several months watching agents fail in production across millions of traces. The failure modes look different on the surface, but underneath they're the same shape: none can be caught by looking at an action on its own. Each is defined by a comparison against something the action itself doesn't carry. There are four things an action gets compared against. What the agent was told. What already happened in the run. What was established as true. What the user took away. Every silent failure below is a mismatch against one of these four references. Rendering diagram… Here's what they all look like. What the agent was told Three of the seven modes are failures against instructions. These instructions come in two kinds: obligations say do X , constraints say never do Y . Together they produce three different failures: an obligation left unmet, an action with no obligation behind it, and a constraint broken. Skipped Work The agent was prompted to do something. For some reason it didn't do it. No error or exception appeared, it just didn't. This is the hardest failure mode to catch in production. The agent returns a response, and that response is plausible. It acknowledges the task, and then the task never gets done. The agent often does adjacent work. It answers a related question, completes nearby subtasks, and fills the hole with something close enough to feel correct. Sometimes it goes further and reports the work complete: logs a confirmation, returns a receipt, or claims it updated a record that was never written. By the time the user notices, the context is gone. What the execution layer sees is a completed turn. Tokens in, tokens out. There's not a signal that an obligation was left open. Catching such events requires holding what the agent was asked against what it did, across the full conversation. You need to track the instruction as a stateful object, follow it through the interaction, check whether it was fulfilled, and whether the agent's claim about fulfilling it is true. This is bigger than a trace problem. Traces tell you what the agent executed. They don't tell you what was supposed to execute and didn't, or that the agent said it did. Out of Scope Work The agent did something but nobody asked it to. Skipped work is an obligation opened and never closed. This is the inverse: an action runs that no obligation ever opened. The agent did something. However, nothing in the task called for it. Sometimes that's a wasted step, an agent modifying a resource it was never scoped to touch, or taking an action with side effects the user never authorized. The agent has a goal and a set of capabilities, and nothing structurally binds the second to the first. Nothing says "only take actions the task actually requires." So when a path to the objective runs through an action that was never in scope, the agent takes it, the same way it finds a way past an ambiguous rule. The action is available, so it's on the table. Here, the execution layer sees a completed action with no error, because doing extra isn't an error to anything watching in the span. Catching it requires holding the action against the full set of obligations in force and asking whether any of them called for it. If nothing did, that's the flag. Instruction Violation Simply put, the agent broke an explicit rule it was given. For example, a rule was given in the system prompt. To the human reader, it's explicit and unambiguous. However, the agent reasoned its way past it, and found a path to its goal that the rule should have blocked, took it, and returned success. The reason this happens is structural. A system prompt isn't a hard boundary, it's a soft constraint living inside the same reasoning loop as the goal. When the goal is concrete and the constraint is ambiguous, the goal wins. What matters is that compliance is relational: the same action is permitted or prohibited depending on the rule in force when it ran. A violation isn't defined by the action alone. An agent that concludes a rule no longer applies has already violated the instruction. This is the sharpest articulation of the whole pattern: a violation is not a property of the action. It's a relation between two artifacts, the instruction and the action, that never appear in the same log line. The instruction either lives in a system prompt or an earlier user message. The action lives in the span, many tokens later. No execution signal connects them, because execution monitoring doesn't know the instruction exists. The execution layer sees a completed action. Catching it requires the instruction and the action to exist in the same evaluation context. What already happened in the run The next two modes use the run's history as their reference. They compare the current action against earlier errors or previous attempts. Integration Failure This one partially surfaces in execution monitoring. Here you can see the error, but you can't see what the agent did about it. For example, a tool call errored, but nothing in the agent's behavior shows it dealt with that. The detectable property is precise: an error occurred and there's no visible failure handling. The surface behavior varies (sometimes the agent masks the error and reports success; sometimes it just stops), but the underlying failure is the same thing: an error existed and the handling didn't. The absence of recovery is the failure. That's a judgement about behavior, not an error code. Error monitoring is responsible for telling you that a tool call failed, not whether the failure is handled, and you need both. Retry Loop The agent repeatedly attempts the same action despite receiving the same failure. This looks like a performance problem. Latency spikes, cost anomalies, spinning. It is one. But the root failure is behavioral: the agent has no stopping condition for repeated failure. It keeps trying because trying is what the objective tells it to do. Unlike the other failure modes, this one has an immediate price tag. Every failed attempt becomes part of the prompt for the next one, growing the context each time. As a result, cumulative cost grows quadratically, not linearly. Every unnecessary retry increases both the size of the next request and the total bill. The execution layer sees elevated latency and higher token usage, and maybe an eventual timeout. It sees each individual error, but not the behavioral pattern producing them. The repetition pattern itself is only visible if you're watching across spans within the run, not solely at the run level. What was established as true One mode is measured against what's actually grounded: the facts established by the context, the tools, and the conversation. Hallucination The agent asserts something with no basis in fact. A feature that doesn't exist, a policy never set, a number never established. It's stated as plainly as if it were true. Where the others check against the task or the run, hallucination needs a grounding check: the claim against the context, the tool responses, the state the agent actually had. Different reference, same shape. A claim measured against something the action itself doesn't carry. The execution layer sees a clean LLM call. Valid tokens, coherent prose, no error code for "this is false." Catching it requires a grounding check. The output is compared against what was actually established, and unsupported claims are flagged. What the user took away The last mode isn't about the agent's work at all. The work was correct. The reference is the user's understanding of it. Communication Failure This happens when the agent did the work but the user thinks it didn't. Communication is part of the task. An agent that does the work and can't convey it hasn't finished. It doesn't break, but it breaks your evaluation metrics. Consider the following: the task was completed and the output was correct. But the agent buried the confirmation, described the work in terms the user didn't recognize, or answered a different framing of the question than the one asked. The user comes back with "you didn't do X." The work is there. Nothing in the response told them so. Communication failures generate support tickets, negative feedback, churn signals, and downstream business costs. They make a working agent look broken. If you're using user feedback as a proxy for agent quality, they pollute that signal in both directions. You're penalizing correct behavior without realizing it. The execution layer sees a completed action, but user feedback sees a failure. Neither is inherently wrong. They measure completely different things. Catching this failure requires detecting the space between what the agent produced and what the user understood, which means watching the conversation after the agent's turn. The strongest signal is a user follow-up that contradicts what the agent actually did, though it takes interpretation, since the user can also simply be mistaken. The Boundary Four references, seven failure modes, one shape. None can be detected by inspecting an action in isolation. Every one is a comparison against a reference the action itself doesn't contain. What execution monitoring actually catches Failure mode error latency cost What the agent was told Skipped work Out of scope work Instruction violation What happened in the run Integration failure Retry loop What was established as true Hallucination What the user took away Communication failure present sometimes 5 of 7 failure modes produce no execution signal at all. Only one of these references is local to the action itself. Integration failure is the exception: the error exists right inside the span, even if confirming no recovery happened means looking further. Every other failure depends on information outside the span. A single action cannot tell you whether an obligation was left open, whether an action ran without authorization, whether identical failures have repeated, whether a claim was grounded in anything real, or whether the user misunderstood completed work. That's the boundary. Execution monitoring evaluates what happened inside the span. These failures are defined by relationships to information outside it. Why This Discontinuity Exists Traditional software has a fixed specification. A test compares the output against that specification and either passes or fails. Agents don't. Their instructions are written in natural language, and they change as the conversation unfolds. A user can add a new requirement, amend an earlier one, or revoke it entirely. That means the correctness of an action depends on when it happened. The exact same action may be correct at one point in the conversation and incorrect later because the instructions changed. This is why a single pass over the transcript can't assign fixed grades to spans. The evaluator has to reconstruct which instructions were in force when each action happened, not simply inspect actions in isolation. How This Ties into Production Monitoring The seven failure modes point to the same conclusion: some production failures cannot be detected from local execution signals alone. Detecting them requires reconstructing the appropriate reference and evaluating the action against it. Concretely, that means four things execution monitoring doesn't: tracking each instruction across the full conversation, not just reading it as context evaluating every action against the instructions that were live at the moment it ran grouping recurring failures across traces, because one instance of skipped work is noise, but the same pattern across many runs is a product incident doing it automatically, across every trace, without being told in advance what failure looks like That last point is the one that matters most. The failure modes above aren't things you know to look for until after they've burned users. The monitoring layer has to find them without being told what to find. That's what we're building at Lemma .

title: 11 Best International Payroll Providers for Global Workers

Business leaders need solutions that handle global workforce payments without regulatory missteps or delays. The best international payroll providers offer comprehensive platforms that streamline these processes while ensuring accuracy and compliance. Effective solutions go beyond basic features to deliver reliable global payment capabilities. Companies need platforms that integrate contractor management, payroll, and compliance tools to efficiently support international teams. Choosing the right payroll software transforms monthly payroll from a complex burden into a streamlined process that protects businesses and supports global workforce growth. Payment delays create measurable financial consequences for international workers. The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 found that 45% of workers have experienced payroll delays or errors when working for international companies. These aren't edge cases. They're common enough to affect how people perceive remote work opportunities, and they often stem from payroll infrastructure problems rather than employer intent. Worker satisfaction connects directly to payment reliability and accuracy. Research from Hibob shows that 82% of employees consider accurate and timely payroll critical to their overall job satisfaction. The gap between signing a contract and receiving first payment reveals how worker-centric a platform actually is, with traditional providers often requiring weeks of manual verification while modern systems compress onboarding to days. Currency conversion costs quietly erode contractor earnings over time. Workers can lose 2 to 4% per transaction through unfavorable conversion spreads and forced auto-conversions. For a contractor earning $60,000 annually, this translates to $1,200 to $2,400 lost purely to conversion timing and fees, turning what appeared to be a strong rate into one that diminishes financial position over months. Payment visibility determines whether workers can budget with confidence or manage constant uncertainty. According to Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2026, only 20% of employees worldwide were engaged in 2025, and payment uncertainty contributes directly to the disconnection workers feel from their employment arrangements. Real-time payment tracking eliminates repeated status inquiries and enables actual financial planning. Global workforce engagement remains critically low despite the expansion of remote work. The same Gallup research indicates that the vast majority of workers feel disconnected from their employment arrangements, with payment infrastructure playing a measurable role in that experience. Platforms that provide multi-currency accounts, transparent fee structures, and direct visibility into payment status address these friction points by giving workers control over timing and currency rather than imposing rigid structures. Payroll software addresses these challenges by consolidating payment processing, currency management, and financial tools into a unified infrastructure, reducing administrative friction for both employers and international workers. Why International Payroll Providers Matter More to Workers Than They Think Most workers don't think about payroll infrastructure until something goes wrong . For international workers , these problems occur frequently enough to be a significant issue . Late payments , surprise transfer fees , currency conversion losses , confusing onboarding , and unclear documentation stem from infrastructure problems , not employer mistakes. According to The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 , 45% of workers experience payroll delays or errors when working for international companies . These issues shape how people perceive remote work overall . 🎯 Key Point: Payroll infrastructure directly impacts worker satisfaction and retention rates for international teams. " 45% of workers have had payroll delays or errors when working for international companies ." — The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 ⚠️ Warning: Poor payroll experiences can damage your company's reputation among global talent before you even realize there's a problem. How do payment delays impact international workers? Payment delays create financial stress . When a contractor in Brazil expects payment on the 30th but receives it on the 5th due to banking holds or compliance reviews, that five-day gap can mean missed rent, overdraft fees, or strained household budgets. The payroll provider's processing timeline determines whether workers can plan their lives with confidence or must manage cash flow uncertainty. What hidden fees reduce worker earnings? Transfer fees and foreign exchange spreads reduce earnings. A worker might agree to a $5,000 monthly rate, but after intermediary bank fees, currency conversion markups, and payment processing charges, they receive $4,750. That $250 difference compounds over time. The best international payroll providers minimize these losses by offering clear fee structures, competitive exchange rates, and direct deposit options that eliminate unnecessary intermediaries. How does onboarding friction delay worker income? Onboarding friction delays income before the first payment. Contractors often face weeks of paperwork, tax form submissions , and compliance verifications before earning. Some payroll systems require extensive documentation upfront without clear explanations of why each piece matters or how long approval will take. Why does payment transparency matter for international workers? Traditional payroll systems lack clear information about payment arrival and status, making it difficult for freelancers and contractors to plan finances across multiple income sources. The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 found that 68% of employees consider on-time, reliable payment essential to job satisfaction. Reliable payments signal that employers respect their workers and value their contributions. How do cross-border payments create additional friction? Managing earnings across borders compounds the challenge. Different currencies , banking systems , payment methods, and regulations create additional complexity. Some payroll providers offer multi-currency accounts, instant notifications, and clear dashboards showing exactly when money will arrive. Others require workers to contact support repeatedly to learn their payment status. This difference determines whether international work feels seamless or exhausting. What makes the best payroll systems stand out? The best payroll systems improve payment reliability, increase transparency, reduce administrative friction , and provide flexibility for managing cross-border earnings . Workers who understand how payroll infrastructure affects their experience can make better decisions about which companies to work with, though most learn this only after something goes wrong. Knowing payroll matters is only half the story. The harder question is figuring out what separates a good provider from one that looks good on paper. A strong international payroll provider makes it easy for workers from the time they start their job, through following the rules for how they get their earnings . You can see the difference in how fast it works , how clear everything is, how many choices workers have , and how confident workers feel on payday . 🎯 Key Point: The best international payroll providers excel in four critical areas : speed of processing, transparency in communication, flexibility in payment options, and reliability that builds workers' confidence. "Workers who receive their pay through efficient international payroll systems report 85% higher satisfaction with their employer's payment processes." — Global Payroll Survey, 2024 💡 Best Practice: Look for providers that offer real-time payment tracking , multiple currency options , and 24/7 customer support to ensure your international workforce feels valued and supported regardless of their location. Geographic Reach That Matches Opportunity Companies hire talented workers wherever they can find the right skills, which means they need payroll infrastructure that works with employees across dozens of countries. When a payroll system doesn't cover enough places, it creates problems: contractors in unsupported areas face delayed payments, higher fees, or must route money through services that take additional cuts. According to Bolto's Global Payroll Solutions Guide , 73% of companies report payroll errors when managing international payroll independently, often because they combine multiple systems to cover different regions. The best providers offer direct payment options across 100+ countries, reducing the steps between employer and worker. Speed Without Sacrificing Reliability Predictability matters more than most people realize. Workers plan rent, bills, and expenses around expected payment dates. When funds arrive late, even by a few days, it creates cascading problems: overdraft fees , missed payments, and damaged credit. Modern payment infrastructure has significantly compressed timelines, but providers vary in speed. Some rely on banking networks that take three to five business days to settle cross-border transactions, while others use faster payment systems that deliver funds within hours. The best providers combine speed with consistency, so workers know exactly when to expect payment and can trust that the schedule will be maintained month after month. Compliance That Protects Both Sides International payments involve rules about taxes, worker classification, identity verification, anti-money laundering compliance, and employment laws. Without adequate support for these requirements, both companies and workers face complications. Strong payment providers automate paperwork collection, verify identities efficiently, and maintain regulatory-compliant records, enabling faster onboarding and preventing payment delays or tax issues. Onboarding That Doesn't Waste Time The payroll experience starts before the first payment. Many workers face lengthy setup processes involving contracts, verification, tax forms, and payment setup. Digital workflows streamline this through automated document collection, instant identity verification, and centralized dashboards, where workers complete everything in a single session. When onboarding takes hours rather than days, workers start earning sooner, and companies fill roles faster. Financial Tools That Go Beyond Payroll The strongest providers recognise that workers need more than a bank transfer. They need flexibility to manage earnings across different currencies, access funds through multiple channels, and make financial decisions suited to their situation. Platforms like payroll software offer contractors global accounts that let them hold multiple currencies, choose when to convert funds, and access earnings via local bank transfers, digital wallets, or payment cards. This eliminates the need for separate accounts or expensive currency exchange services. The third category recognizes that payroll extends beyond moving money from employer to worker—it encompasses what happens after funds arrive . For workers , this distinction matters significantly . A provider might excel at compliance documentation while creating unclear , slow , or expensive payment experiences . ADP Global Payroll ADP represents the traditional enterprise approach to payroll, with infrastructure built for scale and complexity across numerous countries. Key strengths Large-scale payroll infrastructure with decades of operational history . Global compliance support backed by legal and tax expertise. Enterprise payroll administration for high transaction volumes. Extensive reporting capabilities with audit trail documentation. Best fit Large organizations with complex payroll requirements that prioritize established infrastructure over speed or innovation in worker experience. 9. Payoneer Workforce Solutions Payoneer focuses on international payments for freelancers, contractors, marketplaces, and businesses, rather than on employment infrastructure. Key strengths Multi-currency support, global payout network reaching contractors in hard-to-access countries, financial tools for independent professionals, and marketplace integrations that automate contractor payments. Best fit Freelancers, contractors, and businesses making international payments who don't need employment infrastructure or EOR services. 10. Skuad Skuad offers global employment, payroll, contractor management, and compliance solutions for distributed teams, handling both traditional employment and contractor arrangements with an emphasis on compliance. Key strengths Global employment services with localized expertise, payroll management supporting multiple worker classifications, compliance support that adapts to regulatory requirements, and centralized international workforce administration. Best fit Organizations are building distributed international teams that need both employment and contractor capabilities. 11. Oyster HR Oyster HR helps companies hire, pay, and manage talent globally through payroll and EOR services, with a focus on a remote-first work culture and operational infrastructure. Key strengths International hiring support for distributed teams. Global payroll integrated with employment services. Employer of Record services for companies avoiding office setup. Distributed workforce management accounting for cultural differences. Best fit Remote-first organizations building international teams and prioritizing cultural alignment and operational infrastructure. Which Provider Actually Works Best? There is no universal best international payroll provider. The question assumes all stakeholders share the same priorities, which they don't. What do workers prioritize in payroll providers? For workers, onboarding speed determines when they start earning. Payment reliability affects whether rent gets paid on time. Clear explanations shape whether workers understand their net earnings after fees and conversions. Currency choices control how much value is lost during transfers. Easy access to earnings determines whether workers can use their money without friction or extra costs. How do employer priorities differ from worker needs? For employers, the calculation differs: compliance support reduces legal risk, geographic coverage determines the talent pool, integrations affect operational efficiency, and workforce management capabilities shape the administrative burden per international hire. Traditional providers focus on employer control and compliance documentation, while newer platforms prioritize speed and worker experience. Some balance both approaches; others do not. Why does worker experience matter for employers? As global work grows, providers combining reliable payroll systems with strong worker experiences are winning. Workers share their experiences. When one contractor receives smooth onboarding, transparent fees, and quick access to funds, while another waits days for payments and loses money to currency conversion, word spreads. Companies ignoring worker experience eventually face recruitment challenges, regardless of compliance documentation. The real question isn't which provider ranks highest on a generic list, but which provider solves the specific friction points your workers face while meeting your operational requirements. What Workers Should Look For Before Accepting International Opportunities The other half of the picture is how you'll receive , access , and control your earnings . title: PSE&G Prepared for Heavy Rain, Strong Winds; Ready to Respond to Potential Power Outages
body_text: Newsroom PSE&G Prepared for Heavy Rain, Strong Winds; Ready to Respond to Potential Power Outages (NEWARK, N.J. – July 17, 2026) – PSE&G is closely monitoring forecasts calling for heavy rain and possible flooding, strong wind gusts and the potential for isolated tornadoes beginning tomorrow afternoon across parts of New Jersey. The company has activated its storm response plan, positioned additional crews and resources throughout its service territory, alerted customers, and is prepared to respond safely and efficiently should severe weather cause power outages. PSE&G has additional line personnel, tree crews and support staff ready to respond if storms damage electric equipment or bring trees and branches onto power lines. Operations personnel will continue to monitor weather conditions and system performance throughout the event, allowing the company to adjust its response to best serve customers as conditions evolve. “Our crews are prepared and ready to respond wherever they are needed,” said Paul Toscarelli, vice president of Electric Operations for PSE&G . “When severe weather moves through our service territory, our first priority is the safety of our customers, our employees and the communities we serve. We've positioned additional crews and resources across our service area so we can respond quickly as conditions evolve. If outages occur, we’ll work around the clock to restore service as quickly and as safely as possible. We first assess damage across our system to determine restoration process. From there, we make repairs in a way that safely restores power to the greatest number of customers as quickly as possible.” Throughout the storm, PSE&G will remain in close communication with county and local emergency management officials and other public safety partners to help coordinate response efforts as needed. Our customer-facing teams, including representatives in the call center and across the company’s communications channels, will remain active to provide updates to customers as conditions change. During the early July storms, we delivered over 10 million messages to customers, including pre-storm email messages on how to stay safe and prepare for a storm as well as text alerts and outage updates during the storm. PSE&G encourages customers to prepare before the storm arrives: Charge cell phones and other essential electronic devices. Keep flashlights and fresh batteries readily available. Avoid using candles whenever possible. Secure or bring inside outdoor furniture, umbrellas, grills and other loose objects that could become airborne in strong winds. If you rely on electrically powered medical equipment, have a backup plan in place. Never touch or approach downed power lines . Always assume they are energized and dangerous. Stay at least 30 feet away and report them immediately. Use portable generators only outdoors and well away from windows, doors and vents to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning . Customers who rely on electricity to operate life-sustaining medical equipment should notify PSE&G in advance by visiting pseg.com/life or calling 1-800-436-7734 , and should have a backup plan in the event of an outage. Customers can report outages and monitor restoration progress by: Using the PSE&G mobile app Visiting pseg.com/outagecenter Texting “OUT” to 4PSEG (47734) Calling 1-800-436-PSEG (7734) Customers are encouraged to sign up for outage alerts to receive updates by text, email or phone and follow us on social media: @PSEG on Facebook and Instagram and @PSEGdelivers on X. PSE&G reminds customers that restoration work begins only after conditions are safe for crews to perform their work. During widespread outages, crews first assess damage across the electric system to determine restoration priorities before beginning repairs. Restoration efforts focus first on repairing damage that returns power to the greatest number of customers, while also restoring service to critical facilities such as hospitals, emergency response agencies and other essential infrastructure. PSE&G will continue providing updates through its Outage Center, mobile app and social media channels as conditions warrant. If the severity of the storm or its impacts change significantly, the company will provide additional information as it becomes available. For additional storm safety information, outage updates and restoration information, visit pseg.com/outagecenter . ### About PSE&G Public Service Electric & Gas Co. is New Jersey’s oldest and largest gas and electric delivery public utility, as well as one of the nation’s largest utilities. PSE&G has won the ReliabilityOne ® Award for superior electric system reliability in the Mid-Atlantic region for 24 consecutive years. In 2025, for the fourth consecutive year, J.D. Power named PSE&G number one in customer satisfaction for residential electric service in the East among large utilities. PSE&G is a subsidiary of Public Service Enterprise Group Inc., (PSEG) ( NYSE:PEG ), a predominantly regulated infrastructure company named to the Dow Jones Best in Class Index for North America for 18 consecutive years ( www.pseg.com ). Contacts : Media Relations DL-ENT-pseg.communications@pseg.com

title: Kforce Named a 2022 Top Workplace
summary: Kforce’s people-centered culture once again received national recognition, earning Top Workplaces USA 2022 awards for innovation, work-life flexibility and five other areas of excellence. Learn More.
body_text: The solutions firm was named a 2022 Top Workplaces USA, meriting awards in seven focus area TAMPA, FL (November 2022) — Kforce’s people-centered culture once again received national recognition, earning Top Workplaces USA 2022 awards for innovation, work-life flexibility and five other areas of excellence. Kforce was also named an overall Top Workplaces USA for the second consecutive year. The recognitions came as the firm reimagined how and where work is done in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. “We are intentionally charting a new path forward, where flexibility and choice are supported by trust and technology,” Kforce President and CEO Joe Liberatore said. “The result is a powerful combination: the firm is experiencing record-breaking success, and employees are designing their best life-work balance.” The solutions firm, which specializes in technology and other professional staffing services, deepened its connection with its employees over the past several years. Investments in engagement tools and ongoing pulse surveys kept the firm united amid changing times. And an award-winning recognition team ensured employee appreciation and engagement stayed a priority. Leadership listened to employee feedback to shape its technology-enabled hybrid work model, called office occasional . In 2022, the company kept innovation at the forefront, deploying new technologies and leveraging Microsoft’s dynamic ecosystem to strengthen connections in an increasingly dispersed world. The firm also rolled out several key employee-based initiatives, such as listening sessions, stay interviews, a DE&I Council, affinity groups and additional leadership development courses. In addition to the overall company recognition, the solutions firm earned seven Top Workplaces Culture Excellence awards celebrating specific focus areas. All awards were based solely on employee feedback gathered from more than 27 million employees at 70,000 organizations, according to Energage, the research company behind the program. Kforce was honored as a national leader in innovation, employee appreciation, work-life flexibility, employee well-being, professional development, leadership and purpose and values. Top Workplaces awards are based on a research-backed, 24-item employee engagement survey. Earning the national recognition is “a sign of resiliency and impressive performance,” according to Energage CEO Eric Rubino. “When you give your employees a voice, you come together to navigate challenges and shape your path forward,” Rubino said. “Top Workplaces draw on real-time insights into what works best for their organization, so they can make informed decisions that have a positive impact on their people and their business.” ABOUT THE AWARDS Leadership celebrates organizational leaders who inspire confidence in employees and the company direction. They listen to what matters most to employees and use that insight in decision making. Innovation recognizes organizations that have created a culture where new ideas are encouraged, which helps employees to reach their full potential and benefits performance. Work-Life Flexibility recognizes organizations that have built a culture that enables employees to meet the demands of their personal lives while maintaining high performance. Purpose & Values celebrates organizations that have successfully communicated the company mission and integrated those aspirations into the culture. Employee Well-Being celebrates organizations who put the health and wellness of their employees at the center of their workplace culture. Employee Appreciation celebrates organizations who demonstrate gratefulness for the efforts of employees, and that employees reciprocate by being motivated to give their best at work. Professional Development celebrates organizations who focus on developing their employee’s careers and enable them to grow professionally. ABOUT ENERGAGE Making the world a better place to work together. TM Energage is a purpose-driven company that helps organizations turn employee feedback into useful business intelligence and credible employer recognition through Top Workplaces . Built on 16 years of culture research, Energage delivers the most accurate competitive benchmark available. With access to a unique combination of patented analytic tools and expert guidance, Energage customers lead the competition with an engaged workforce and an opportunity to gain recognition for their people-first approach to culture. ABOUT KFORCE Kforce is a solutions firm specializing in technology and other professional staffing services. Each year, we provide career opportunities for approximately 30,000 highly skilled professionals on a temporary, consulting or direct-hire basis. These experts work with roughly 3,000 clients, including a significant majority of the Fortune 500, helping them conquer challenges and meet their digital transformation goals. Together, we reimagine how business gets done. For more than 60 years, we’ve achieved our clients’ objectives by combining a KNOWLEDGEforce®—our namesake—with flexibility and an unmatched drive for excellence. MEDIA CONTACT Alexa Rodriguez Public Relations Manager 813.552.1817 | arodriguez3@Kforce.com
